lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning the organiser of a weekend food festival to book a stall. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 4.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 4.

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: Good morning, Harbourside Food Festival, Dan speaking.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Oh, hi. I saw on your website that you've still got a few stalls available for the festival in June, and I'd like to book one, if that's possible.

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: Yes, we've got a handful left, so you're in luck. I'll fill in the booking form as we go. Can I start with your name?

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Sure. It's Grace Thornbury.

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: Thornbury. Is that B-E-R-R-Y at the end, like the fruit?

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: No, it's B-U-R-Y. So the whole thing is T-H-O-R-N-B-U-R-Y. Everyone gets that wrong, don't worry.

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: Got it, thanks. And what kind of food will you be selling?

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: I run a small business from my kitchen at home. Last year I was doing noodles as well, at the farmers' market, but it was too much work for one person, so now it's just dumplings.

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: Lovely. We haven't got anyone doing those yet, so you should be busy. Now, stall sizes. We've got stalls that are two, three or four metres wide. Which would you like?

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: I was going to say two metres, because it's only me. But I'm bringing a fridge with me this time, so I'd better go for three.

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: Three metres, then. That's our most popular size. And is there anywhere in particular you'd like to be? Most people ask to be near the stage, but I'm afraid that area's fully booked already.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: That's fine, it's a bit noisy there anyway. What about somewhere near the entrance?

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: Hmm, the entrance is mostly taken by the bigger food vans. But I do have a space next to the fountain, right in the middle of the square. Lots of people sit around it to eat.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Oh, the fountain sounds perfect. I'll take that one.

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: Great, I'll put you down for it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 5 to 10.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions 5 to 10.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: So, can you tell me how much it costs?

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: Sure. You can book for just one day, which is 120 pounds, or for the whole weekend. The weekend price was 180 pounds last year, but it's gone up a little, so it's now 210 pounds.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: I'll do the whole weekend, I think. Is electricity included in that?

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: Not quite. The price covers the stall itself and a table, but electricity is extra. We charge 15 pounds for each socket you need. With a fridge, you'll probably want two.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Okay, two sockets, then. Do you need any documents from me before the festival?

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: Yes, just one. Because you're preparing food, we need a copy of your food hygiene certificate. Could you email it to us by the end of May? Your insurance papers you can simply bring with you on the day.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: No problem, I've got that somewhere. And what time should I get there on the Saturday?

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: Traders can drive onto the square from six in the morning. But the public come in at eight, and every vehicle has to be off the square by then, so don't leave it too late.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Right, I'll aim to arrive at six, then. Is there anything I should know about packaging? At the market I usually use plastic boxes.

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: Ah, that's changed this year. Plastic isn't allowed at all now. And last year we said recyclable was fine, but now all takeaway containers have to be compostable. There are some good local suppliers, and I can send you a list.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Yes, please, that would be really helpful. And finally, where do I park once I've unloaded?

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: A lot of traders use the station car park because it's closer, but it's pay and display and it fills up fast. We've arranged free parking for stallholders in the car park behind the library, so I'd go there. It's only about a five-minute walk.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Brilliant. I think that's everything I needed to ask.

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: Okay, Grace. I'll send you a confirmation email with a payment link this afternoon. See you in June!

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Thanks very much, Dan. Bye.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part 2. You will hear the manager of a student residence talking to a group of new tenants. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 17.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 17.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to Larchfield House. I'm Megan Doyle, the residence manager, and my office is the one just behind reception. I know you've all had a long day of unpacking, so I'll try to keep this short, but there are a few things you really do need to know before you settle in.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: Let's start with your rent, because it's the thing I get asked about most. A lot of you seem to think your rent covers a gym membership. That was true until last year, but the university changed the deal, so now you just get a discount at the sports centre if you show your residence card.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: What your rent does include is contents insurance, so if your laptop or your phone is stolen from your room, you're covered, as long as the door was locked. Please don't pay for a separate policy, as some students did last year without realising.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: The kitchens on each floor are cleaned every weekday by our staff. Your bedrooms, though, are your own responsibility, and we do check them once a term. The laundry is in the basement, and the machines cost two pounds a wash, which you pay through the residence app.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: Right next to the laundry you'll find the bike store. You don't need to pay anything extra for that, it's part of what you're already paying for, but please register your bike at reception so we know whose it is.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: Now, let me tell you about the shared facilities in the building. First, the study room on the ground floor. It never closes, so you can use it at any hour of the day or night. People often ask me whether they need to book a desk, but you don't. Just turn up and find a free seat.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: Then there's the roof terrace. It isn't new, actually, it's been there since the building opened, but a surprising number of residents don't know it exists. The views are wonderful. It's open from eight in the morning until sunset, so not at night, partly for safety and partly out of respect for our neighbours. It had some work done on the railings over the summer, but that's all finished now.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: On the first floor there's a music practice room, which is fully soundproofed. Some people assume they can just drop in whenever they like, but it's very popular, so you'll need to reserve a slot on the app beforehand. You can have it for up to two hours at a time.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: Next, the common room, with the big screen and the sofas. You're welcome to eat in there, as long as you clear up after yourselves. It's also the only place in the building where you can bring friends who don't live here. They'll need to sign in at reception, though.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: And finally, the games room. I'm sorry to say the pool table there is out of use at the moment. Someone damaged the cloth last week, and we're waiting for a specialist to come and fix it, so it'll be a couple of weeks before you can play.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 18 to 20.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions 18 to 20.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: Okay, a few practical points. Fire safety first. The alarm is tested once a week, so if you hear it ringing for about thirty seconds at that time, there's no need to leave. It used to be Monday mornings, but so many of you had nine o'clock lectures that we moved it, and now it's every Wednesday at two in the afternoon.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: Separately, there's a full evacuation drill once a term, and that one isn't announced in advance. So if the alarm goes off at any other time, you must leave the building straight away.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: Next, key cards. If you lose yours, please don't come to reception first, because they can't issue new cards anymore. What you need to do is report it on the residents' website straight away, so we can switch the old card off. You can then collect a new one the next working day.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: There is a ten-pound replacement fee, but you don't pay that at the time. It's simply added to your next rent payment.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: And lastly, some advice for your first week. On Friday there's a pizza night in the common room, which is great fun, but it's entirely optional. You'll also hear about the residents' committee, but elections for that aren't until November, so there's no rush.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: If you only do one thing this week, go and knock on the door of the resident assistant for your floor. They're all second- or third-year students, they've lived here themselves, and they're the people who'll help you most when something goes wrong. Right, that's all from me. Any questions?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

lines.speaker: tutor
lines.text: Come in, both of you. So, you're presenting on vertical farming next month. How's it going?

lines.speaker: chloe
lines.text: Pretty well, I think. We've done most of the research, and we've decided to organise the middle section around the different crops that are grown in vertical farms, because that's what people find easiest to picture.

lines.speaker: tutor
lines.text: Good idea. Which crops are you including?

lines.speaker: owen
lines.text: Five, so far. We start with lettuce. Most people would guess it's the crop that makes vertical farms the most money, but actually the profit on lettuce is pretty low.

lines.speaker: chloe

lines.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the history of the telescope. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: Good morning. Today I'm going to trace the history of the telescope, from a curiosity sold at markets to the machines we now send into space. And I want to start with a slightly surprising fact, which is that the telescope wasn't invented by an astronomer at all.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: The earliest telescopes we have records of appeared in the Netherlands around 1608, and they were the work of spectacle makers. Their workshops were full of lenses of different strengths, so it's not hard to imagine one of them holding two of them up in a line and noticing that a distant church tower suddenly looked much closer.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: What's revealing is how the device was first sold. Nobody was thinking about the stars. A tool that let you see an enemy's ships or soldiers hours before they could see you was obviously valuable to governments, so the telescope was offered, above all, as a military instrument. Its value for navigation and trade came a little later.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: News of the invention spread remarkably fast, and within a year Galileo in Italy had built his own, improved version. When he turned it to the night sky, he found mountains and craters on the Moon and saw that Venus has phases, just as the Moon does.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: But the discovery that caused the most trouble was four small moons circling Jupiter. At the time, the accepted view was that every heavenly body moved around the Earth. Here was clear evidence that some objects did not, and that was a very uncomfortable idea for the authorities of the day.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: Now, these early instruments all used lenses, and lenses have a basic weakness. Glass bends different colours of light by slightly different amounts, so they never come to a focus in exactly the same place. The result was that every bright star or planet appeared surrounded by coloured fringes, which made fine detail very hard to see.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: Astronomers found that the effect was reduced if the lens was very weakly curved, but that meant the telescope had to be extremely long. By the 1670s, some were more than forty metres in length, with the lens hung from a tall pole and the observer standing far below. They were, as you can imagine, almost impossible to use in any kind of wind.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: The real breakthrough came from Isaac Newton, who reasoned that a mirror reflects all colours in the same way. So in his telescope, he replaced the main lens with a curved mirror, and the coloured fringes disappeared. This design, the reflecting telescope, is the ancestor of nearly every large research telescope in use today.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: However, there was a practical problem. Good glass mirrors couldn't be made yet, so the mirrors were cast from a polished alloy of copper and tin. This reflected less than two thirds of the light that hit it, and worse, it soon became tarnished, so mirrors had to be taken out and repolished every few months, which often ruined their shape.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: The solution only arrived in the 1850s, when chemists found a way of depositing a very thin layer of silver onto a surface. From then on, telescope mirrors were made of glass coated with silver, which was lighter, far more reflective, and could simply be re-coated when it lost its shine.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: With good mirrors available, telescopes grew rapidly in size, and astronomers also began to think much more carefully about where to put them. In the early twentieth century, major observatories were moved out of universities in the middle of cities and up onto mountains. The thin, dry air was part of the reason, but the main aim was to get far away from the light pollution of growing cities, which washed out faint objects.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: Size, though, brought its own difficulties. A single mirror more than about eight metres across sags under its own weight and distorts the image. So the largest modern telescopes don't use one mirror at all. Instead, the mirror is made of dozens of hexagonal segments, fitted together like tiles, with each one adjusted by computer many times a second.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: The final step, of course, was to leave the Earth altogether. Even from a mountain top, the atmosphere is never completely still, and its turbulence is what makes stars appear to twinkle. A telescope in orbit avoids that entirely and produces images of extraordinary sharpness.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: But it has one great weakness: if anything goes wrong, a space telescope is extremely difficult to repair. When the Hubble Space Telescope was launched in 1990, its mirror turned out to have a tiny error in its shape, and it took a mission by astronauts three years later to correct it. Next week, we'll look at telescopes that don't collect visible light at all.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

paragraphs.text: Until a few centuries ago, the streets of most towns were almost completely dark once the sun had set. Anyone who needed to go out after nightfall had to bring their own light, usually a burning torch made from rope soaked in tar or a simple lantern containing a candle. In larger cities such as London, those who could afford it paid a 'link boy' to walk ahead of them carrying a flame. From the fifteenth century onwards, a number of European towns passed rules requiring householders to hang a lantern outside their front door on winter evenings. Candles were costly, lanterns were frequently stolen, and the wind often blew the flames out within an hour. Lighting was also limited to certain nights. Officials consulted the calendar and did not require lamps on any night when there was expected to be a full moon, on the assumption that moonlight alone would be enough.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more organised approach emerged in the second half of the seventeenth century. In 1667 the authorities in Paris began installing several thousand lanterns, hung from ropes stretched across the streets, and paid for them through a special tax rather than relying on the goodwill of individual households. Other cities soon copied the idea, and over the following century the candle gave way to the oil lamp. The most successful designs were fitted with polished metal reflectors, which directed the light down onto the road and allowed lamps to be placed much further apart. Even so, Ellery points out, streets remained gloomy by modern standards, with small pools of light separated by long stretches of near darkness.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The real transformation came with gas. When coal is heated in a sealed container, it gives off a gas that burns with a bright flame, and in 1807 a stretch of Pall Mall in London became the first public street to be lit in this way. The gas was produced at a central works and carried to the lamps through a network of underground pipes. Each evening a lamplighter walked a fixed route, using a long pole to open the valve and light each lamp, and he returned at dawn to put it out again. Gas lamps were several times brighter than oil lamps, and within a few decades most large British towns had adopted them. Not everyone welcomed the change. Ellery has found that some residents feared explosions, while certain doctors warned that artificial light would tempt people to stay up late, to the detriment of their health. Shopkeepers, by contrast, were enthusiastic, because brightly lit streets encouraged customers to keep shopping well into the evening.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Electric lighting arrived in the late 1870s in the form of the arc lamp, which produced light by passing a current across a small gap between two carbon rods. Arc lamps were so dazzling that they were often mounted on tall iron towers, each intended to illuminate several streets at once. Their light, however, was harsh and bluish, and the carbon rods burnt away so quickly that they had to be replaced every day. In the early twentieth century the incandescent bulb, which gave a softer and warmer light, gradually took over. Electric lamps could be switched on from a central point, and later by automatic timers, so the lamplighter became a figure of the past. In some cities, however, a small number of gas lamps were kept in historic districts as a reminder of an earlier age.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The next significant development was driven less by the needs of pedestrians than by the motor car. From the 1930s, and especially after 1950, engineers began to light main roads with sodium lamps, which give off a characteristic orange-yellow glow. Sodium lamps were highly efficient, producing far more light per unit of electricity than earlier bulbs, and they rarely needed attention. Their great weakness was colour: under their light, almost everything appears in shades of yellow and grey, making it difficult to tell a red car from a brown one. The lighting standards of this period were drawn up mainly with drivers in mind, specifying how brightly the road surface should be lit rather than how safe a footpath felt to someone walking home.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Since the early 2000s, cities around the world have been replacing sodium lamps with light-emitting diodes, or LEDs. LEDs use considerably less electricity, produce a white light in which colours look natural, and can be dimmed or brightened remotely. When the city of Brennholt converted its 28,000 street lamps between 2012 and 2015, its lighting energy costs fell by more than half, according to Lukas Arndt, the engineer who oversaw the project. Yet the switch has raised new concerns. Early LED lamps gave off a cold, bluish-white light, and researchers have linked such light to disturbed sleep among people living nearby and to confusion among night-flying insects and migrating birds. Astronomers, too, complain that the night sky over cities is brighter than ever. In response, some local authorities now dim or switch off the lights in quiet residential streets after midnight, an approach that, as Ellery observes, would not have seemed strange to the townspeople of five centuries ago.

passage.title: Slowing the rise of resistant bacteria

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When penicillin entered widespread use in the 1940s, it was hailed as a miracle drug, and for several decades new antibiotics arrived quickly enough to keep medicine ahead of the bacteria they were designed to kill. That position no longer holds. Resistance is not a failure of medicine but a predictable consequence of evolution: whenever an antibiotic is used, the few bacteria that happen to survive it are left to multiply, and the genes that protected them spread. At the same time, the discovery of entirely new classes of antibiotic has slowed dramatically since the 1980s. Faced with a growing number of infections that respond poorly to treatment, researchers and policymakers have pursued several quite different strategies. Some aim to slow the spread of resistance by using existing drugs less; others concentrate on bringing new treatments to patients. Each has its supporters, and each faces objections.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most widely adopted approach is known as stewardship: ensuring that antibiotics are prescribed only when they are genuinely needed, at the right dose and for the right length of time. At Westmere Teaching Hospital, the infectious diseases specialist Dr Ruth Okonjo introduced a simple rule requiring every antibiotic prescription to be reviewed by a senior doctor after 48 hours, by which time laboratory results are usually available. Over two years, antibiotic use on the hospital's wards fell by around a fifth, with no rise in deaths or readmissions. In general practice the challenge is different. Many patients with coughs and sore throats, most of which are caused by viruses, expect to leave with a prescription, and doctors working under time pressure often give way. One response has been 'delayed prescribing', in which the patient is told to collect the medicine only if their symptoms have not improved after a few days. Rapid tests that can tell a bacterial infection from a viral one within minutes would help further, but Okonjo concedes that they remain too expensive for routine use in most surgeries.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second front concerns farming. In many countries more antibiotics are given to animals than to people, sometimes to treat sick animals but often to prevent disease spreading among livestock kept in crowded conditions, and in some places simply to make them grow faster. The European Union banned the use of antibiotics as growth promoters in 2006, and a number of other countries have since introduced similar restrictions. Pieter Vos, an agricultural economist at Lindholm University, studied pig farms that had cut their antibiotic use and found that the most effective changes were not chemical at all. Better ventilation, more space per animal and wider use of vaccines reduced infections so much that antibiotic use fell by more than half, while production costs rose by only a few per cent. Vos accepts, however, that such improvements require investment that many small farmers in low-income countries cannot afford, and that without financial support, strict limits on antibiotics may simply drive them out of business.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Reducing use buys time, but it cannot by itself produce new medicines, and here the obstacle is largely economic. Developing a new antibiotic can cost as much as developing a drug for cancer or heart disease, yet any genuinely novel antibiotic is likely to be held in reserve for the most serious cases, precisely to protect it from resistance. Low sales mean low returns, and several companies that have brought new antibiotics to market in recent years have struggled financially as a result. The health economist Clara Brandt argues that the solution is to separate a company's income from the quantity of the drug it sells. Under the subscription model she proposes, a government would pay a manufacturer a fixed annual fee in return for guaranteed access to a new antibiotic, however much or little of it was actually used. Critics respond that such schemes are expensive for taxpayers and risk rewarding drugs that offer only a slight improvement on existing ones. Brandt's answer is that payments should depend on how far a drug meets a need that no current treatment can satisfy.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A final group of researchers is looking beyond conventional antibiotics altogether. The most discussed alternative is phage therapy, which uses viruses that infect and destroy particular bacteria. Phages were studied in Western Europe and North America in the early twentieth century but were largely abandoned there once antibiotics became available, although their use continued for decades in parts of the former Soviet Union. Their great advantage is precision: a phage attacks only one type of bacterium and leaves the patient's helpful bacteria untouched. The microbiologist Dr Anil Mehra points out, however, that this precision is also a drawback. Before treatment can begin, the bacterium must be identified and matched with a suitable phage, a process that can take several days, and approval systems designed for a single, unchanging chemical compound are poorly suited to treatments that may need adjusting for each patient. For now, Mehra regards phages as a valuable addition to antibiotics rather than a replacement for them, a view that sums up the field as a whole: no single strategy is likely to be enough on its own.

passage.title: Should children still learn to write by hand?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every few years, a newspaper columnist announces that handwriting is finished. Children, the argument runs, now spend far more time tapping on screens than holding pencils, adults rarely write anything longer than a shopping list, and schools that devote hours to forming letters are preparing pupils for a world that no longer exists. Handwriting, on this view, belongs alongside the slide rule and the typewriter: an ingenious tool that technology has made redundant. I think this comparison is mistaken, though not for the reasons usually offered by handwriting's defenders. The real question is not whether children should learn to write by hand, but what kind of handwriting they should learn, for how long, and why.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case against extensive handwriting instruction deserves to be taken seriously. Time in the primary classroom is limited, and every hour spent practising letter shapes is an hour not spent on reading, mathematics or, increasingly, computing. There is also a question of fairness. For children with dysgraphia, a condition that makes the physical act of writing unusually slow and effortful, an education built around pen and paper can make a motor difficulty look like a lack of intelligence. Several education systems have responded to such concerns: Finland, for instance, stopped requiring schools to teach joined-up writing in 2016, choosing to give keyboard skills more attention instead. Those who welcome such changes are right that nostalgia is a poor basis for a curriculum.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Where they go wrong is in assuming that handwriting matters only as a means of producing text. A growing body of research suggests that, for young children at least, forming letters by hand plays a part in learning to read. In one frequently cited study, the developmental psychologist Ingrid Solberg taught two groups of four- and five-year-olds a set of unfamiliar letters, one group by copying them with a pencil and the other by finding them on a keyboard. Several weeks later, the children who had written the letters were noticeably better at recognising them. Solberg's explanation is that drawing a letter forces the child to attend to the features that distinguish it from similar letters, whereas pressing a key involves an identical movement whatever the letter. Her study involved fewer than forty children and measured recognition over a short period, so it falls well short of proof. Still, it is consistent with other findings, and it points to a benefit that typing does not obviously replace.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The evidence from older students is more often cited and, in my view, more often misread. Marcus Hale, an educational psychologist, compared university students who took lecture notes on laptops with those who wrote them by hand. When tested a week later, the two groups did about equally well on factual questions, but those who had written by hand performed better on questions that required them to explain and connect ideas. Hale's laptop users, it emerged, had tended to record the lecture almost word for word, while the slower handwriters had been forced to decide what was worth keeping. The finding is usually presented as a victory for the pen. Yet what it actually demonstrates is the value of selecting and summarising, and there is no obvious reason why a typist who deliberately limited what she recorded could not obtain the same benefit. It is an argument for teaching students how to take notes, not for any particular instrument.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If the case for handwriting is stronger than its critics allow, the way it has traditionally been taught is harder to defend. In many schools, a great deal of effort still goes into joined-up writing and into neatness for its own sake, with pupils praised or corrected according to how elegant their pages look. The research I have described offers no support for this. The benefits for early reading appear to come from forming individual letters, not from joining them, and I know of no convincing evidence that cursive script brings any cognitive advantage over a fluent, legible print. What matters is that handwriting becomes automatic: a child who must think about how to shape each letter has little attention left for what she is trying to say. On this point, Finland's decision seems to me entirely sensible.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What would a reasonable policy look like? First, children should be taught to write by hand thoroughly in their early years, with the aim of reaching that automatic fluency rather than producing beautiful pages. Second, keyboard skills should not be left to chance. Children who are never taught to type tend to develop a slow 'hunt-and-peck' style, searching for each key and pressing it with one or two fingers, a habit that is hard to unlearn later. Touch-typing, in which the fingers find the keys without help from the eyes, should therefore be taught systematically from around the age of eight. Neither skill need be sacrificed for the other; the hours freed by abandoning the pursuit of elegant cursive would go a long way towards paying for both.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There remains the matter of assessment. In many countries, important examinations are still written by hand, which means that a pupil who cannot write quickly is penalised regardless of what she knows. Allowing such pupils to type their answers would remove an obstacle that has nothing to do with the subject being tested. None of this amounts to a sentimental defence of handwriting, nor to a call for its abandonment. Handwriting is a tool, and like any tool it should be judged by what it does. The evidence suggests that for young children it does something useful, which is reason enough to keep teaching it, and to teach it better.
